anthropic-pentagon-retaliation-ruling.headline: Judge rules Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic
anthropic-pentagon-retaliation-ruling.body_md:
A federal judge has told the Pentagon it cannot punish an AI company for refusing to let its chatbot be used for autonomous weapons or domestic surveillance — at least not by branding the firm a national security threat and hoping nobody asks too many questions about why.

In a 59-page ruling issued Thursday night, US District Judge Rita Lin found that the Department of Defense's decision to label Anthropic a "supply chain risk" — a designation Congress built for firms suspected of ties to foreign adversaries — was unlawful retaliation against a company that had simply said no to the military's terms. The order came down hard: the designation was, Lin wrote, "arbitrary and capricious," issued without the constitutional process Anthropic was owed, and driven by motives the government is not allowed to act on.

![The Pentagon, headquarters of the US Department of Defense](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bf/The_Pentagon%2C_Headquarters_of_the_US_Department_of_Defense.jpg)

## A contract that ran into a red line

The dispute traces back to last summer, when the Pentagon awarded Anthropic — alongside Google, OpenAI and xAI — a contract worth up to $200 million to speed the military's adoption of AI tools. Anthropic's version came with conditions attached: its acceptable-use policy barred Claude from being deployed in autonomous weapons without a human in the loop, and from mass surveillance of Americans.

That clashed with what the Pentagon actually wanted, which was unrestricted access — "all lawful use cases," in the contract language the two sides fought over for months. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei held the line, telling the administration the company "cannot in good conscience accede" to stripping the safeguards, and arguing the restrictions touched only "high-level usage areas,” not the operational decisions commanders make in the field.

![Dario Amodei, Anthropic co-founder and CEO](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/35/Dario_Amodei_at_TechCrunch_Disrupt_2023_04.jpg)

## Blacklisted for saying no

The administration's answer came on February 27, when President Trump directed federal agencies to "immediately cease all use" of Anthropic's technology. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth followed by ordering the Pentagon to designate the company a supply-chain risk — a status that, under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act, exists to let the government excise contractors and products believed to be conduits for foreign espionage or sabotage. It is not, on its face, a tool for settling policy disagreements with a vendor over how its own software gets used.

Anthropic called it exactly that in lawsuits filed in March in both San Francisco and Washington, describing the move as an "unlawful campaign of retaliation." At a July 30 hearing, Judge Lin signaled where she was headed, telling government lawyers their position looked "at odds ... with the First Amendment" and calling it "really troubling."

![Pete Hegseth, US Secretary of Defense](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/29th_United_States_Secretary_of_Defense_Pete_Hegseth_Official_Portrait_2025.jpg)

## "Arrogance is not a legal basis"

Lin's written order lands on a specific, almost blunt finding: the Pentagon's actions, she wrote, "were based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its 'arrogance' in criticizing the government, not based on any articulable basis to believe that Anthropic would actually sabotage its model." Neither the Constitution nor the statute the administration invoked, she found, lets officials "impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic's critique of the Administration's views."

What seems to have undercut the government's case most was its own inconsistency. Lin pointed out that officials were simultaneously trying to have it both ways — floating a plan to classify Anthropic as essential infrastructure under the Defense Production Act, continuing contract talks, and working with the company on cybersecurity projects, all while publicly branding it a threat to national security. A company genuinely suspected of sabotage is not usually also being courted for critical-infrastructure status.

Anthropic's response was measured: "We welcome the court's ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful." The Pentagon is expected to appeal, and a parallel case Anthropic filed in Washington, D.C. is still working its way through the courts.

## What the ruling actually settles

The practical effect, for now, is that the supply-chain risk label comes off and contractors barred from working with Anthropic can resume doing so. The larger effect is a marker in the sand: a court has said the government cannot reach for national-security tools to punish a company for exercising editorial control over its own product, even when that product is being sold to the military. Given how many AI firms now hold defense contracts with similar human-in-the-loop and surveillance carve-outs, the ruling gives them a legal argument — not just a moral one — the next time an agency threatens to make an example of a vendor that won't remove its guardrails. Whether it holds depends on the appeal, and on the D.C. case still ahead.

whatsapp-crime-cash-investigation.headline: Investigation finds WhatsApp chats used to funnel crime cash
whatsapp-crime-cash-investigation.body_md:
A cross-border investigation by public broadcasters including the BBC has traced how WhatsApp group chats are being used to run informal money-transfer networks — known as hawala — that move cash for drug traffickers, people smugglers and, in some cases, extremist financing. The reporting, coordinated through the European Broadcasting Union's investigative journalism network, does not allege that Meta built or condoned the system. It shows something more mundane and more awkward for the company: ordinary, unencrypted-by-design group chat features are being used as the coordination layer for a decades-old underground banking method, at a scale that runs into hundreds of millions of euros.

One former money launderer, given the pseudonym "Frank," told reporters he had personally handled transactions totalling several hundred million euros. He described his introduction to the system at an office outside Rotterdam, where five or six couriers arrived within about 90 minutes carrying at least €1 million between them — instructions on where and when relayed, he said, over WhatsApp. "It's not just about money," he told the EBU. "It's about the financing of terror. It's about drug trafficking. It's about prostitution and all sorts of other crap."

In Vienna, police raided what they called the city's biggest hawala office, run out of a kebab restaurant. Two Syrian brothers who operated it were convicted of human trafficking, torture and rape after a courier who lost €350,000 was tortured to recover the debt; they were sentenced to 18 and eight years respectively. Gerald Tatzgern, who leads human-trafficking investigations at Austria's Criminal Intelligence Service, was among the officials who worked the case. Separately, Austrian police and Europol dismantled a smuggling ring, financed through the same informal channels, that had moved an estimated 100,000 people into Europe over 18 months.

## Encryption wasn't even the issue

What makes the WhatsApp findings uncomfortable for Meta is that none of this required breaking end-to-end encryption — it simply exploited group chats as a free, ubiquitous coordination tool, the same reason legitimate businesses use them. That is a harder problem to regulate away than a technical vulnerability, and it lands while WhatsApp is already fielding unrelated regulatory heat in Britain: Ofcom opened a formal probe in January into whether Meta gave it complete and accurate data on WhatsApp's business-messaging practices during a market review. Meta said it took the request seriously and would cooperate. The company has not issued a specific response to the hawala findings.

The timing matters. The Financial Action Task Force, the global anti-money-laundering standard-setter, used its June plenary to approve two forthcoming reports — one on hawala and underground banking networks, due in September, and a separate one on how terrorist financing is conducted through social media and instant-messaging apps. Neither will name WhatsApp specifically, but both give governments a template to press platforms for more proactive monitoring of exactly the kind of group activity this investigation documents. For Meta, the practical question is whether that pressure stays at the level of guidance, or turns into the kind of binding disclosure and monitoring obligations that have already cost it dearly on child-safety grounds.

china-climate-plan-coal.headline: China's new climate plan lands alongside a coal-power surge
china-climate-plan-coal.body_md:
Beijing spent late July unveiling the most comprehensive climate policy document it has produced in over a decade. It spent the first half of the year connecting more new coal-fired power capacity to the grid than it had in the previous ten years combined. Both things are true, both happened under the same government, and together they say more about China's actual energy priorities than either headline does alone.

The five-year plan, released by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment together with 18 other central departments, sets out what officials call the "main policy instrument" for China's climate action through 2030: a target to cut carbon dioxide intensity — emissions per unit of GDP — by 17% over the period, a reaffirmed pledge to peak emissions before 2030, and a new goal to push electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35% by the end of the decade. It also commits to trimming 30 million tonnes of non-CO2 greenhouse gases, mainly methane from coal mines, by 2030.

![Wind turbines at a power plant in Xinjiang, China](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e0/Wind_power_plants_in_Xinjiang%2C_China.jpg)

None of that is new in substance. Analysts at Carbon Brief describe the plan as a consolidation exercise rather than a step up in ambition — it restates commitments Xi Jinping made at the United Nations climate summit last September, when he pledged to cut net greenhouse gas emissions 7-10% below peak levels by 2035 and lift non-fossil fuels to more than 30% of energy consumption. What makes the document notable is its scope: for the first time, a five-year plan builds a single target framework spanning CO2, other greenhouse gases, carbon markets and adaptation, rather than scattering climate goals across separate industrial and energy plans.

## The coal counter-narrative

While the plan was being finalised, China's power sector was moving in the opposite direction. New research from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) and Global Energy Monitor puts new coal-fired capacity commissioned in the first half of 2026 at 30 gigawatts — up 43% on the same period last year — against just 2.7 GW retired. Coal-fired generation itself rose 3.4% year-on-year even as individual plants ran fewer hours on average, evidence that new capacity is arriving faster than the system needs it.

A further 274 GW of coal plants sit in the pipeline, equivalent to 22% of China's existing operating fleet, which at roughly 1,270 GW already accounts for more than half of the world's coal power capacity. Much of what came online this year traces back to a wave of permits issued during the 2021-2025 plan period, when 112.8 GW of coal capacity was approved in 2023 alone — projects now simply reaching completion on schedule, regardless of what the new climate plan says about the years ahead.

"Coal capacity is still growing because of legacy approvals and policy protections, even as plants run fewer hours," said Qi Qin, a CREA China analyst. Christine Shearer of Global Energy Monitor put it more bluntly: new coal plants keep entering operation "supported by market mechanisms that guarantee coal both capacity payments and significant electricity sales."

![A coal-fired power plant in Shuozhou, Shanxi province, China](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3e/Shuozhou_coal_power_plant.JPG)

## Paid to sit idle

That reference to capacity payments points to the real mechanism at work. China's National Development and Reform Commission revised its capacity-payment rules this year, raising the fixed-payment share from 30% to 50% of a plant's costs and rebranding the scheme the "reliable capacity compensation mechanism." It now extends to batteries and gas alongside coal, but coal remains its biggest beneficiary — plants are effectively paid to exist as backup generation for a grid managing record but volatile renewable output, whether or not they burn much fuel.

The volatility is real. Wind and solar curtailment — clean electricity generated but discarded because the grid can't absorb it — rose to 360 terawatt-hours in the first half of 2026, up 49% year-on-year, and by itself exceeded the entire increase in power demand over the period. Beijing's stated logic is that firm capacity, chiefly coal, is needed to back up intermittent renewables and cover peak demand during heatwaves and cold snaps until storage and grid infrastructure catch up. Critics, including researchers at CREA, counter that the country is building redundancy it will have to strand: paying to keep plants standing while wasting the very clean power those plants were meant to complement.

## Two plans, one government

The tension is not hidden — it's arguably by design. The new climate plan explicitly pledges to "peak coal use" during 2026-2030, an implicit admission that coal use is still rising and needs to be capped rather than cut. That framing lets Beijing claim climate credentials — record renewable build-out, a 17% carbon-intensity cut, an economy-wide emissions ceiling — while its energy planners keep approving coal as insurance against blackouts, grid instability and the political cost of an outage during a heatwave.

For investors, the read-through is less about whether China is abandoning its climate targets — it isn't — and more about pace and sequencing. Chinese utilities and coal-plant operators are locking in another five years of guaranteed capacity revenue, a floor under coal-sector valuations that pure decarbonisation narratives tend to miss. Renewables developers, meanwhile, are absorbing the cost of curtailment: generation that gets built, connected and then discarded doesn't earn. Both dynamics can persist simultaneously, and the new plan does nothing to resolve which one dominates as the decade wears on.

The next test comes at the UN climate conference, where China's follow-through on its 2035 pledge — the 7-10% emissions cut below peak, the 30%-plus non-fossil energy share — will be measured against whatever the coal pipeline data shows for the second half of 2026. CREA and Global Energy Monitor are expected to publish updated fleet figures early next year; a pipeline still running at 274 GW by then would suggest Beijing's "peak coal use" pledge is arriving later, and at a higher plateau, than the plan's language implies.

brown-united-ireland.headline: Gordon Brown says a united Ireland is coming
brown-united-ireland.body_md:
Gordon Brown does not do backseat driving, he insisted this week — right before climbing into the passenger seat and grabbing the wheel.

In an interview with The Guardian's Saturday magazine, timed to the release of his new book, *The Future Starts With Us*, the former prime minister was asked whether the land border between Northern Ireland and the Republic meant unification simply made sense. His answer was unhurried but unambiguous: "Yes. Well, of course, in the long term, Ireland will be united." He called it "a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing," and drew a pointed contrast with Scotland, where he has long argued the economic and geographic case for staying in the UK is overwhelming. Northern Ireland, in his telling, is a different kind of case entirely.

![Gordon Brown speaking at a podium](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a9/Gordon_Brown%2C_UK_Prime_Minister.jpg)

## Into Burnham's line of fire

The timing was not incidental. Brown's comments landed days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a united Ireland referendum was "off the table" — a remark that Downing Street has since been trying to walk back into something less absolute. Brown, who was Tony Blair's chancellor when the Belfast Agreement was signed in 1998 and prime minister in 2010 when policing and justice powers were devolved to Stormont, has more standing than most retired politicians to weigh in on this particular question. That he chose to do so, gently contradicting the sitting prime minister within days of Burnham's own remarks, is the real story here — not the forecast itself, which he offered no timeline, polling or mechanism for.

The reaction has split along familiar lines. Sinn Féin's Mary Lou McDonald said no prime minister has the right to "high-handedly" write the unity referendum provision out of the Good Friday Agreement. The DUP's Gavin Robinson took the opposite reading of Burnham's original remarks, saying they had "put to bed the nonsense" of unity-poll speculation. In Dublin, junior minister Niamh Smyth said she "categorically and fundamentally" disagreed with Burnham. Brown's own comments have simply given each side fresh ammunition rather than resolving anything.

## What the agreement actually says

Under the Good Friday Agreement, it falls to the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland — currently Chris Bryant — to call a border poll, and there is a duty to do so if unification looks likely to command majority support. Any actual change would then need separate majorities in both Northern Ireland and the Republic. None of the ingredients for that test exist today: no fresh polling was cited alongside Brown's remarks, no economic modelling, no government working group. What exists is a well-regarded former PM using a book tour to nudge a debate that Burnham had just tried to close down.

The next marker to watch is not a poll or a bill but whether Burnham's government offers a fuller account of what "off the table" actually means in practice — and whether Brown's intervention pulls more Labour figures into a debate Number 10 would clearly rather avoid this side of an election.

ai-voice-clone-law-campaign.headline: Actors launch campaign for a UK AI voice-clone law
ai-voice-clone-law-campaign.body_md:
More than 80 actors, comedians and audiobook narrators have written to Prime Minister Andy Burnham asking for something that sounds almost too basic to need legislating: the right to own your own voice.

The campaign, called Save Our Voices Now, is backed by Hugh Bonneville, Matt Lucas, Nicola Coughlan, Luke Evans, Jen Brister, Siobhán McSweeney and Pearl Mackie, among others. It wants a statutory right — held by every UK resident, not just working performers — to control whether an AI system can clone their voice. Alongside the open letter, organisers have launched a petition on the government's own petitions site, the standard route for forcing a subject onto the floor of the Commons if it clears 100,000 signatures.

> "My voice is unique, it's mine, it's part of my identity. So is yours. That's worth speaking up about." — Hugh Bonneville

## Why performers are worried

Voice-cloning tools have got good enough, and cheap enough, that a few seconds of audio is now sufficient to generate a convincing fake. Equity, the performers' union, says it has filed claims on behalf of more than 20 members whose voices it believes were used without permission — enough, the union says, that unauthorised cloning has become one of the main issues it now handles day to day. The problem isn't confined to actors: campaigners cite a figure of 28% of UK adults reporting they've been targeted by a voice-cloning scam, typically fraudsters impersonating a relative in distress.

Audiobook narrator Alice Sockett, one of the campaign's co-founders, has called the practice "an existential threat to our entire industry," pointing to narrators whose voices are used to generate synthetic audiobooks with no fee and no consent.

## What the law would actually do

The campaign's ask is narrower than it might sound. Rather than a blanket ban on synthetic voices, it wants a personality right — similar to image rights in some jurisdictions — that requires consent before a voice is cloned and gives people standing to sue or demand takedown when it isn't. Organisers point to Denmark, which recently amended its copyright law to give individuals ownership over their face, body and voice, with the ability to force removal of unauthorised AI-generated content and to claim compensation. So far, the UK government's response has amounted to a promised consultation rather than a bill, leaving the timeline open.

That gap matters commercially. A statutory consent requirement would land directly on voice-synthesis startups and the media companies licensing their tools — forcing provenance checks, consent records and takedown processes that smaller developers may struggle to build quickly. If Westminster follows Denmark's lead, the practical effect is likely to favour better-capitalised players who can absorb compliance costs, while raising the bar for entrants relying on scraped or unlicensed training audio.

The next marker is the government's consultation, still without a published date, and whether the petition clears the 100,000-signature threshold that would guarantee a Commons debate. Until then, the campaign's leverage is star power rather than law.

halliburton-brazil-deepwater.headline: Halliburton lands integrated Brazil deepwater appraisal deal
halliburton-brazil-deepwater.body_md:
There is a version of this story where a giant oil discovery becomes a giant contract, and Halliburton is not the giant. It is the plumber called in after the architect draws the blueprint — necessary, well paid, and entirely unglamorous.

BP has awarded Halliburton an integrated drilling and evaluation contract for the first appraisal campaign at Bumerangue, the deepwater block in Brazil's Santos Basin that BP has called its largest oil and gas discovery in 25 years. Neither company disclosed the value or duration of the deal, which Halliburton confirmed this week and which several trade outlets, including Offshore Technology and World Oil, reported after BP's announcement.

## From wildcat well to workhorse contract

Bumerangue made headlines a year ago, not this week. BP's exploration well, drilled roughly 404 kilometres off Rio de Janeiro in water more than 2,300 metres deep, struck a hydrocarbon column ultimately estimated at around 1,000 metres — a thin oil cap sitting atop a much thicker gas-condensate layer, in pre-salt carbonate rock spanning more than 300 square kilometres. BP put potential oil and gas in place at 2.4 billion barrels of oil equivalent, with roughly 500 million barrels considered recoverable. It was, by any measure, a genuine elephant find in a basin many geologists had assumed was thoroughly picked over.

What happens now is the less cinematic part of the business: figuring out exactly how much of that resource is real, producible, and worth developing. That is appraisal work, not production, and it is where Halliburton comes in.

![Halliburton offices in Houston, Texas](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/76/HalliburtonBellaireBlvdOfficesHouston.JPG)

## What Halliburton is actually being paid to do

The contract bundles well planning, drilling and formation evaluation into a single package, with Halliburton also deploying its LOGIX automation platform — software that uses real-time downhole data to adjust drilling parameters on the fly — alongside AI-assisted analytics intended to give BP faster reads on reservoir quality as the campaign progresses. Francisco Tarazona, Halliburton's senior vice-president for Latin America, framed the award as proof of the company's ability "to execute complex deepwater projects through a combination of digital solutions, integrated service delivery, and local expertise."

That is standard vendor language for what is, in essence, standard vendor work. Appraisal drilling in a basin as structurally complicated as the Santos — layers of salt, carbonate reservoirs, water depths that punish equipment — is technically demanding, but it is also the kind of contract Halliburton wins regularly in Brazil. The company already runs completion and stimulation work for Petrobras in the same basin, and picked up a separate deepwater automation job with Eni in Indonesia only last month. Bumerangue is a new logo on a familiar client list, not a new business line.

## Why the market shrugged

Simply Wall St's read on the deal is blunt: it reinforces the narrative around Halliburton's digital-services push without changing the underlying investment case. Analyst models built around the stock still hinge on the company reaching something like $25 billion in revenue by 2029 through modest, multi-year growth — figures a single appraisal contract, undisclosed in value, does not move. Halliburton shares showed no meaningful reaction to the news, consistent with a deal that industry press covered as a routine operational update rather than a catalyst.

That is the more useful way to read this story than as a Halliburton headline at all. It is really a Bumerangue update, filtered through the mechanics of how oil majors actually develop a discovery: years of appraisal wells, seismic reprocessing and service contracts before anyone talks seriously about first oil. BP has not yet sanctioned development at the field, and appraisal campaigns of this scale typically run multiple years before a final investment decision.

The next marker worth watching is not anything Halliburton does — it is whether BP, having now lined up its appraisal contractor, starts talking timelines for a development decision at Bumerangue itself.

drumcree-parade-ruling.headline: Court ruling reopens Drumcree parade dispute, stoking NI fears
drumcree-parade-ruling.body_md:
The last time the Orange Order marched down the Garvaghy Road, in 1997, it took a wall of riot police and CS gas to get several hundred Orangemen past the nationalist residents lining the route. The ban that followed — imposed in 1998 by the newly created Parades Commission — has held for every one of the twenty-eight summers since. This week a Belfast High Court judge tore it up, and Northern Ireland's political class immediately started arguing about whether that means anything at all.

![The Church of the Ascension at Drumcree, near Portadown, where the Orange Order's annual parade begins](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0e/Drumcree_Church_2018-07-26_-_1.jpg)

> "I have no hesitation in making the quashing order. This is simply a case that does not stand up to any scrutiny at all."

So said Mr Justice McAlinden, ruling on a judicial review brought by a Portadown Orangeman against the Commission's latest determination barring the Order's Portadown District from completing its traditional route past Drumcree church and along the Garvaghy Road. The Commission itself conceded the point: not all six of its members had signed off on the final determination before it was issued, and the judge's ruling notes further irregularities, including reliance on anonymous social media comment and an unaddressed factual error about a local MP's involvement. Counsel for the applicant, John Larkin KC, called it a "scandalous abdication of responsibilities."

## A narrow ruling, a wide reaction

What the judgment does not do is authorise a parade. It quashes one flawed decision and sends the Commission back to redo its homework — a point the Commission itself was quick to stress, saying the ruling "does not affect any future considerations and decisions" on parades along the route. The Order is expected to lodge a fresh application, most likely for next July's marching season, and the Commission will have another chance to reach the same conclusion by a cleaner process.

That legal nuance has done nothing to calm the politics. Gavin Robinson, the DUP leader, called the outcome "a totemic victory, which has laid bare why confidence in the Parades Commission has collapsed within the unionist community," and some unionists are now demanding Commission members resign. Sinn Féin's John Finucane accused unionist politicians of a "tribal and triumphalist" response, saying he sees "no logic or justification" for reviving the march. First Minister Michelle O'Neill visited the Garvaghy Road and said residents there feared a return to the violence of the 1990s. Breandán Mac Cionnaith, the nationalist campaigner who led resistance to the parade in the Drumcree years, put it more bluntly: unionists were "playing politics" and creating "nervousness" in the district.

## Why a parade ruling shows up here

Drumcree was, for the better part of a decade, the clearest annual stress test of the Good Friday Agreement's settlement — a dispute capable of putting thousands of police and soldiers on the streets and souring investor sentiment toward Northern Ireland at the margin. Its return to the news cycle is not, on its own, a market event: there is no parade yet, no date, and the legal process that produced this ruling is explicitly about procedure rather than the merits of the ban. But Northern Ireland's political stability has occasionally shown up as a modest risk premium in sterling and gilt-adjacent sentiment during past flashpoints, and the last time this dispute ran hot it coincided with a decade of intermittent violence that unsettled the province's investment case for years afterward.

The more immediate marker to watch is not the ruling itself but the Commission's next determination on a fresh Orange Order application, along with whether any interim marching-season decisions in the coming months reignite street tension before next July's parade actually approaches. Until then, this stays a story about Northern Ireland's politics reopening an old wound, not one with a visible line to asset prices.

burnham-assisted-dying-abstain.headline: Burnham to abstain on assisted dying vote, breaking with Starmer
burnham-assisted-dying-abstain.body_md:
Andy Burnham has decided the one vote he won't cast as Prime Minister is the one that would define him most as a man from Merseyside who has watched his own views shift over two decades in public life.

Downing Street confirmed this week that Burnham will abstain when the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill returns to the Commons on 11 September, telling reporters he does not want to "unduly influence the debate" from the despatch box. It is a conscience matter, he said, and Parliament's decision to make — his job is to implement whatever MPs decide, not steer them toward it.

![Prime Minister Andy Burnham, pictured at 10 Downing Street](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/67/Prime_Minister_Andy_Burnham_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg)

The decision is notable mostly for who it isn't. Keir Starmer, the man Burnham replaced in Downing Street in July after a bruising Labour leadership contest, voted in favour of the bill both times it came before the Commons — at second reading in November 2024 and again at third reading last June, when it passed narrowly, 314 votes to 291. Starmer's yes was itself notable: a sitting Prime Minister putting his name behind a piece of deeply contested private members' legislation rather than staying above it. Burnham, by contrast, is choosing to stay above it entirely.

## A bill that keeps coming back

The legislation itself has had an unusually long road. Sponsored originally by backbench Labour MP Kim Leadbeater, the bill would let terminally ill adults in England and Wales with fewer than six months to live apply for an assisted death, subject to sign-off from two doctors and an independent panel. It cleared the Commons last summer only to run aground in the House of Lords, where a small number of peers tabled hundreds of amendments and effectively talked out the session. With time up, the bill fell.

It is now back as a fresh bill for the 2026–27 session, reintroduced by Lauren Edwards MP and due its Commons stage on 11 September. Should it pass again, the Parliament Act means the same handful of peers won't be able to block it a second time — which is precisely why the coming vote matters more than the procedural label of "second reading" suggests.

## Cabinet still split

Burnham's abstention doesn't paper over the divide inside his own government. Health Secretary Wes Streeting remains opposed, warning the bill risks diverting "time and money" from a palliative care system he considers under-resourced. Edwards has pushed back, arguing better end-of-life care and the right to choose assisted dying "can and must go hand in hand." Burnham has sat somewhere in between: he said last month that fixing the funding of palliative and social care ought to come before Parliament legislates on assisted dying, even while acknowledging his own view has moved, over the years, toward supporting the principle.

That evolution — mayor of Greater Manchester to backbencher to Prime Minister within a matter of weeks this summer — is part of what makes the abstention read as more than procedural caution. A free vote lets MPs vote their conscience without the whip; a Prime Minister declining to use his own vote is a step further, an explicit renunciation of the informal weight a PM's declared position carries over undecided colleagues.

## Why it travels beyond Westminster

For an ostensibly domestic, moral-conscience question, the vote has drawn interest from life-sciences and healthcare investors watching for signals on how assisted-dying regulation might shape palliative care commissioning, hospice funding and the broader end-of-life care market in England and Wales. A government that won't state a preference is, in that narrow sense, a government whose regulatory direction on the issue remains genuinely unsettled — not a strategic ambiguity but an actual one. More broadly, a Prime Minister stepping back from a fight this consequential may embolden backbenchers weighing rebellion on other fronts, at a moment when Burnham's government is already governing without much room for error.

The vote itself lands on 11 September. Whether it passes will turn less on Burnham's absence from the lobby than on the roughly three dozen MPs still undecided since June — the same margin that separated 314 from 291 last time.

ashley-burnham-high-street.headline: Mike Ashley attacks Burnham's 'populist' High Street plans
ashley-burnham-high-street.body_md:
Mike Ashley does not do quiet disagreement. The Frasers Group founder, never a man to let a government policy pass without a verdict, has written to Downing Street to tell Andy Burnham that his plan to revive Britain's high streets is populist window-dressing — good for a headline, bad for anyone actually running a shop.

The proposals in Ashley's sights are the centrepiece of the prime minister's retail pitch ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget on 28 October: a review of business rates for pubs and hotels, a new levy on warehouses to fund lower rates for bricks-and-mortar retailers, a crackdown on "fake" discounting, plus the more consumer-facing sweeteners — a £2 bus fare cap and the removal of VAT from household electricity bills.

![Mike Ashley, the Frasers Group founder, in 2008](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8d/Mike_Ashley_at_Tup_Tup_Palace.jpg)

> "Rather than address the real underlying issues... it is easier for you to pick topics which provide good media soundbites and the old salve of yet more regulation."

That is Ashley's assessment of the government's approach in the letter, which brands the warehouse levy "delusional" and warns that shortsighted or populist reactions to genuine business challenges are not the answer. His objection to the warehouse tax is straightforward economics as he sees it: warehouses are where a huge share of modern retail — his own online operations very much included — actually make their margin, and taxing them harder to subsidise the high street risks simply pushing costs onto the shopper the policy claims to protect. He is similarly unimpressed by Burnham's rhetoric on "rip-off Britain" discounting, arguing that markdowns are precisely the mechanism by which retailers make goods cheaper, not a trick played on customers.

## Part of a wider grumble

Ashley is not shouting into a void. Earlier the same week, Phones 4u founder John Caudwell and the former Marks & Spencer and Asda chairman Lord Stuart Rose put their names to the "Stop the Creep" campaign, a business-founder coalition pressing the government to reverse the rise in employers' National Insurance, restore entrenched entrepreneurial tax reliefs, and rule out fresh levies on dividends, capital gains and business assets ahead of the Budget. Rose said he had "never been more concerned about the cost of doing business", with tax and regulation now "serious impediments to growth and employment".

![Prime Minister Andy Burnham](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Prime_Minister_Andy_Burnham_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg/960px-Prime_Minister_Andy_Burnham_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg)

Burnham, for his part, has told the Financial Times he intends to tackle the "challenging" cost of doing business and has tried to head off fears that October's Budget will bring another tax raid on firms already smarting from previous increases. That reassurance sits awkwardly next to a warehouse levy explicitly designed to raise money from one part of retail to subsidise another — the kind of redistribution that tends to please whoever isn't paying it and infuriate whoever is.

## Noise, not yet a movement

What Ashley's letter amounts to, for now, is one very rich, very online retailer restating a view he has held for the better part of a decade: that business rates and regulatory tinkering are a distraction from the deeper structural problems — footfall, rents, online competition — that have hollowed out Britain's town centres. It is a familiar complaint from a familiar source, and it stops well short of the sector uniting against the government the way pension funds or gilt markets might.

What gives it weight is timing and company. Landing in the same fortnight as the Caudwell-Rose intervention, it reads less like an isolated grievance and more like an opening skirmish in the run-up to the Budget, with business groups trying to shape the narrative before Healey's numbers are even drawn up. Whether that pressure changes anything in the Treasury's plans is the more interesting question, and one that won't be answered until 28 October.

The next marker to watch is whether other major retailers — the ones without Ashley's taste for a public letter — put their names to similar warnings before then, or whether this stays a fight fought by a handful of outspoken billionaires while the rest of the industry keeps its head down.

man-city-gakpo-transfer.headline: Man City in advanced talks for Liverpool's Cody Gakpo
man-city-gakpo-transfer.body_md:
Cody Gakpo scored Liverpool's equaliser-that-wasn't-quite on Saturday, teeing up Alexander Isak for a simple tap-in against Nottingham Forest, then trooped off midway through the second half and watched his side draw 2-2. By Sunday afternoon he was the subject of an £85m tug-of-war between Liverpool and Manchester City, with the transfer window slamming shut in under 48 hours.

City have opened advanced talks over a deal worth more than £85m ($115m) and have been encouraged that Gakpo is receptive to a move to the Etihad, with personal terms already under discussion between the player's camp and the club. Liverpool, who had spent most of the summer insisting the Dutch international was not for sale, are now understood to be prepared to let him go — but only once they have banked his replacement.

![Cody Gakpo playing for Liverpool](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/93/Cody_Gakpo_04012026_%281%29.jpg)

## A rebuild chasing a rebuild

The irony is thick. Manchester City are in the market for Gakpo because they spent the summer dismantling their own attack: Savio departed for Tottenham in a club-record £75m deal, Omar Marmoush followed him to north London for around £60m, and further down the spine Rodri left for Barcelona, Bernardo Silva and John Stones exited on free transfers, and Tijjani Reijnders moved to Saudi Arabia's Al-Qadsiah. It is the heaviest turnover at the Etihad since Pep Guardiola arrived a decade ago — fitting, perhaps, since Guardiola isn't the one picking the team anymore. Enzo Maresca, poached from Chelsea in the close season, is overseeing the reconstruction, and has been candid about the gaps left behind. "This is a squad that doesn't need to do many things," he said last week. "At the same time, the club lost important players in terms of experience — Bernardo, John, Nathan, different players. So for sure there are things that we need to do." City are also chasing Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr as a second wide option, but Gakpo, a proven Premier League goal threat with 18 goals and six assists in his first season under previous manager Arne Slot, is the priority.

Liverpool's own reshaping under new head coach Andoni Iraola — the Spaniard who replaced Slot this summer after three seasons turning Bournemouth into European qualifiers — explains why a deal that would have been unthinkable in June is now plausible. Liverpool are on the verge of signing Bradley Barcola from Paris Saint-Germain for £106m, rising to £123m with add-ons, on a five-year contract, and have already added Victor Munoz from Osasuna, who scored a stunning equaliser of his own against Forest on his Anfield debut. Only once Barcola's move is registered, sources indicate, will Liverpool sanction Gakpo's exit. Asked about his squad's shape with the window closing, Iraola offered little: "Now we have two or three days and we will see what happens with everyone."

## What's next

The Premier League's summer window closes at 11pm BST on Tuesday, and both deals — Gakpo out, Barcola in — are racing the same clock, with a completed deal sheet offering clubs a two-hour grace period to finish paperwork if talks run long. Matchday two continues regardless: Chelsea host Brighton, Manchester United face Ipswich Town, and Sunderland meet Fulham, all before deadline day dawns. Whether Gakpo lines up for City this season, or Liverpool decide £85m still isn't enough to sell a direct rival their most in-form forward, should be settled by Tuesday night.
